title: Restarting a Citroën 2CV4: engine, gearbox, driveshafts and the checks that finish the job properly
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: Once the structure is sound again, the 2CV4 needs a logical recommissioning order: brakes and suspension first, then engine, gearbox, driveshafts, sealing and ignition before any real test drive.
content:
On this 2CV4, the mechanical work was not treated as a reward at the end of the project. It was handled as a chain of systems that had to be brought back into agreement after the underside was repaired: brakes, suspension, engine, gearbox, driveshafts and sealing. That order matters. On a non-running classic, hearing the engine too early proves very little if the rest of the car is not ready to carry it.

Make the rolling side safe before the engine

The first method of recommissioning starts with the parts that hold the car on the road: brakes, suspension, spring cans, dampers and obvious wear points. On this 2CV4, those areas were tackled before anyone thought about a real return to the road. A car that starts but does not brake or track properly is not recommissioned; it has been woken up too early.

The same rule matters for the budget. Safety parts define the real framework of the first tests. Without them, any engine start remains an isolated gesture with no reliable follow-up.

Rebuild the engine and observe the ignition choice correctly

The engine of this 2CV4 was rebuilt with new cylinders, pistons and head work. That changes the mechanical base in a visible way: compression returns, sealing improves and the flat-twin becomes easier to inspect at start-up. Again, the value of the work lies in what was opened and checked, not in the bare fact that the engine can fire.

The electronic ignition also deserves to be assessed for what it is: a discreet improvement in regularity and ease of starting, not a change of character. On a 1974 2CV expected to run with the family, that kind of measured deviation can save maintenance time without distorting the whole car.

Gearbox, driveshafts and sealing belong to the same chain

The gearbox was removed, opened for inspection and made tight again with a full set of oil seals. The driveshafts followed with new gaiters and a general overhaul. This work is less visible than paint, yet it decides whether the first miles will validate the project or produce a fresh round of leaks and dismantling.

On a small front-wheel-drive car, the relationship between engine, gearbox and driveshafts has to be considered as one single chain. If one link remains doubtful, the return to the road quickly turns into a return to the lift.

Validate before the first real miles

Once the mechanical assembly is back together, the cautious method is to check before driving far: no leaks, even braking, ignition setting, fuel delivery, fluid levels, gearbox operation and the general behaviour of the transmissions. A restored 2CV returns to the road when those points agree, not when the engine sounds happy on its own inside the workshop.

The page about this 2CV4 restoration summarises the whole project. The draft on structural metal work explains why mechanical recommissioning only makes sense after the base is sound again.

Static checks come before starting

Old oil is reviewed, the engine turned by hand and the fuel system isolated until tank and hoses are clean. Earth connections, ignition, control free play and cooling tinware are checked before the starter is powered. Establishing lubrication pressure by the appropriate workshop method protects the first rotation better than prolonged cranking on stale fuel.

Validate the transmission without skipping stages

Clutch, gear selection, boots and driveshaft play are checked with the wheels raised and the vehicle securely supported. After starting, initial engagement is made without load, followed by a very short movement in a closed area. Noises on lock, vibration, leaks at gearbox outputs and a heating hub are recorded immediately. Any anomaly ends the test before one defective component damages another.

Road use waits for rebuilt and bled brakes, safe tyres, working lamps and verified running-gear fasteners. First journeys alternate low speed, measured braking and stationary inspections. Levels, seepage, drum temperature and charging voltage form a development log. That follow-up converts a successful start into a genuinely usable car.
